mainTopic: Three readings of 'לא בשמים היא' about acquiring תורה. Then a ברייתא on how a city's outline is set for the תחום שבת, and רב הונא's 4,000-אמה rule for a bow-shaped city.
overview: This amud finishes a section of אגדה about how a person acquires תורה. אבדימי בר חמא בר דוסא reads 'לא בשמים היא' as saying that you must chase תורה even to the heavens or across the sea. רבא and רבי יוחנן read the same verse differently: תורה is not found in arrogant people, in people who think they know it all, or in merchants who are always traveling. Then the גמרא returns to the משנה's topic with a ברייתא. It explains how a city's outline is set, based on the city's shape, before the 2,000 אמה of the תחום שבת are measured from it. The גמרא then goes through the ברייתא line by line, using 'פשיטא' and 'לא צריכא' to show what each rule adds. רב הונא rules that a bow-shaped city is filled in only if its two ends are less than 4,000 אמות apart. The גמרא points out that this seems to contradict his 141⅓ rule for a breached wall, and רבה בר עולא resolves it: one case has a gap on one side, the other is split on two sides. Finally, the גמרא asks why רב הונא needed the breached-wall rule at all, and begins quoting a משנה that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: תורה must be pursued even to the heavens
steps.stepSummary: אבדימי בר חמא בר דוסא reads 'לא בשמים היא' as teaching that one must make any effort needed to reach תורה, and this supports the earlier idea that תורה takes real work.
steps.simpleTranslation: This matches what אבדימי בר חמא בר דוסא said: What does the verse 'It is not in heaven, nor is it beyond the sea' mean? It means that if it were in heaven, you would have to climb up after it. If it were across the sea, you would have to cross over after it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching that backs up what it said just before: keeping your תורה takes real effort. It quotes אבדימי's explanation of the verse 'לא בשמים היא'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says תורה is NOT in heaven. אבדימי reads it as a 'what if': even if it were up in heaven, you would be obligated to go get it. So the verse is a lesson about how much effort a person must be ready to put in.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what [so-and-so] said; it links an idea to a supporting statement
What is the meaning of what is written?
It is not in heaven (דברים ל:יב)
Beyond the sea

steps.confusionAlert: The verse sounds like it means 'תורה is easy and close by.' אבדימי reads it the other way: you would have to chase it even if it were far away. This is a lesson about effort, not about how easy תורה is.

phrases.english: And this is what was said by
phrases.notes: Links back to the previous idea that תורה requires great effort.

phrases.english: Avdimi bar Chama bar Dosa:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"It is not in heaven
nor is it beyond the sea"?
"It is not in heaven" teaches
that if it were in heaven,
you would need to go up after it,
and if it were beyond the sea,
you would need to cross after it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר אַבְדִּימִי בַּר חָמָא בַּר דּוֹסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the aggadic theme from the end of the previous daf: one must work hard to acquire and keep תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person must make any effort necessary, even 'going up to heaven,' to acquire תורה.

steps.title: תורה is not found in those who think they are above it
steps.stepSummary: רבא reads the verse as describing personal attitudes: תורה is not found in someone who feels above it, or in someone who thinks he has mastered all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: 'It is not in heaven' means תורה is not found in someone who lifts his mind above it like the heavens. And it is not found in someone who stretches his mind over it like the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different reading of the same verse. For him, 'heaven' and 'sea' describe two kinds of bad attitude toward learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אבדימי read the verse as a lesson about effort. רבא reads it as a lesson about character. 'Like the heavens' is someone who feels he is above needing a teacher. 'Like the sea' is someone who thinks his knowledge is endlessly wide, as if he already knows everything.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises his mind; feels above it
Widens his mind; thinks he knows it all
It will not be found

phrases.english: Rava said:
"It is not in heaven" means:
it will not be found in one
who raises his mind over it like the heavens,
and it will not be found in one
who widens his mind over it like the sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, different reading of the same verse, focused on attitude rather than effort.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תורה does not stay with someone who feels above it or who thinks he has mastered all of it.

steps.title: תורה is not found in the arrogant or in traveling merchants
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads 'heaven' as arrogance and 'beyond the sea' as merchants who are always traveling and have no time to learn.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: 'It is not in heaven' means תורה is not found in arrogant people. 'Nor is it beyond the sea' means it is not found among merchants or traders.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a third reading of the verse. Each half of the verse describes a different kind of person who will not acquire תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רבא, he reads 'heaven' as a kind of pride: arrogant people. He reads 'beyond the sea' in a practical way. Merchants who travel constantly across the sea do not have the steady time that תורה needs.

keyTerms.meaning: Arrogant people
Merchants who travel around
Traders

steps.whatToRemember: There are three readings of 'לא בשמים היא': (1) אבדימי: chase תורה wherever it is. (2) רבא: it is not in someone who feels above it or who thinks he knows it all. (3) רבי יוחנן: it is not in the arrogant or in traveling merchants.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
"It is not in heaven" means:
it will not be found among the arrogant;
"nor is it beyond the sea" means:
it will not be found among merchants
nor among traders.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: לֹא בַּשָּׁמַיִם הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third reading of the same verse that closes the aggadic section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תורה is not found in the arrogant, nor among merchants and traders who are always traveling.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: how are city boundaries extended?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא opens by asking how we extend (מעברין) the outline of a city for measuring the תחום שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught in a ברייתא: How do we extend the boundaries of cities?
steps.whatsHappening: The aggadic section is over, and the גמרא now returns to the משנה's topic. This line sets up the question that the ברייתא answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before measuring 2,000 אמה for the תחום שבת, we first have to decide where the city's edge is. Cities come in different shapes, so the ברייתא asks how we draw that outline.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught (introduces a ברייתא)
How?
We extend or add to the city's outline (עיבור)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
How do we extend the boundaries of cities?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כֵּיצַד מְעַבְּרִין אֶת הֶעָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the aggadic digression and returns to the halachic topic of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the outline of a city is set, based on its shape, before the תחום שבת is measured.

steps.title: City shapes: long, round, square, and uneven
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives rules for each shape of city: a long city stays as it is, a round city gets corners, a square city gets none, and an uneven city is evened out.
steps.simpleTranslation: A long city is measured as it is. For a round city, we add corners to it. For a square city, we do not add corners. If the city was wide on one side and narrow on the other, we treat it as if it were even.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. It gives a rule for each type of city shape.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is to box the city into a square or rectangle and then measure the תחום from there. A round city is enclosed in a square, which gains the corner areas. A city that is narrow on one side is filled out as if it were wide on both sides. The square case sounds obvious, and the גמרא will soon ask why it needed to be said.

keyTerms.meaning: Long (rectangular) city
Round city
Corners
Square city
We view it as if

steps.whyThisMatters: These rules decide where the 2,000 אמה of the תחום שבת begin. Squaring off a city gives its residents extra walking room on שבת.

phrases.english: A long city: as it is.
A round city: we make corners for it.
A square city: we do not make corners for it.
If it was wide on one side
and narrow on the other side,
we view it as though it were even.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ברייתא's question from step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Long city: as is. Round city: add corners. Square city: no corners added. Uneven city: treated as if both sides were the wider width.

steps.title: Houses that stick out from the city
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if one or two houses stick out from the city's edge, we imagine a string stretched across their outer edge and measure the 2,000 אמה from that line.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one house sticks out like a turret, or two houses stick out like two turrets, we picture a string pulled straight across their outer edge. Then we measure 2,000 אמה outward from that string.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 5 keeps listing shapes of cities. Now it deals with a city where one or two houses stick out past the rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We do not measure from the main edge of the city. Instead, the line is pushed out to the tip of the protruding house, as if a string ran along the whole length of the city at that point. This gives the city a bigger outline, so the residents' תחום reaches farther.

keyTerms.meaning: A turret or bulge: a part that sticks out from a straight line
A stretched string, an imaginary straight line
We view it as if: an imagined legal picture
2,000 cubits, the length of the תחום שבת

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה בַּיִת אֶחָד יוֹצֵא כְּמִין פִּגּוּם,
phrases.english: If one house was sticking out like a turret,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שְׁנֵי בָתִּים יוֹצְאִין כְּמִין שְׁנֵי פִגּוּמִין —
phrases.english: or two houses were sticking out like two turrets,

phrases.aramaic: רוֹאִין אוֹתָן כְּאִילּוּ חוּט מָתוּחַ עֲלֵיהֶן,
phrases.english: we view them as if a string were stretched across them,
phrases.notes: The string runs along the city's length, touching the outer tip of the protruding houses.

phrases.english: and one measures 2,000 cubits from it and outward.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה בַּיִת אֶחָד יוֹצֵא כְּמִין פִּגּוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of city shapes begun in step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Protruding houses extend the city's line; we imagine a string across their tips and measure from there.

steps.title: A city shaped like a bow or the letter gamma
steps.stepSummary: If a city curves like a bow or bends like a gamma (an L-shape), its empty inside area is treated as if it were full of houses, and we measure from the filled-in outline.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the city is shaped like a bow, or like the Greek letter gamma, we picture the empty space inside as full of houses and courtyards. Then we measure 2,000 אמה from that outline.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its list with cities that curve or bend. It fills in the open space so the city counts as one solid block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bow-shaped or L-shaped city has a big empty area between its arms. The ברייתא does not measure from the inner curve. It pretends the gap is built up, so the measurement starts from the straight line that closes the shape.

keyTerms.meaning: A bow: a curved shape
Gamma, the Greek letter Γ: an L-shaped, right-angle bend
Houses and courtyards

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's rules usually enlarge the city's outline before the 2,000 אמה are measured: corners are added to a round city, protruding houses are joined by an imaginary string, and gaps in curved shapes are filled in.

phrases.english: If the city was shaped like a bow
or like a gamma,
phrases.notes: The Greek letter Γ, an L-shape.

phrases.aramaic: רוֹאִין אוֹתָהּ כְּאִילּוּ הִיא מְלֵאָה בָּתִּים וַחֲצֵירוֹת,
phrases.english: we view it as if it were full of houses and courtyards,
and one measures 2,000 cubits from it and outward.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיְתָה עֲשׂוּיָה כְּמִין קֶשֶׁת אוֹ כְּמִין גַּאם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא's list of city shapes.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Bow- or gamma-shaped cities are treated as if the inner gap were filled with houses.

steps.title: Isn't the rule for a long city obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's line 'a long city stays as it is' and asks why it needed saying, since it seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: a long city is measured as it is. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back and studies the ברייתא line by line. It starts by asking why the rule for a long city had to be written at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A long city already has straight edges, so of course we measure from those edges. If a rule seems to say nothing new, the גמרא assumes it must be teaching something, and it asks what that is.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said: the formula for quoting a source the גמרא is about to discuss
Long (here, a long city)
It is obvious! A challenge that a statement seems unnecessary

phrases.english: The Master said: A long city is measured as it is.
That is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: אֲרוּכָּה כְּמוֹת שֶׁהִיא. פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from quoting the ברייתא to analyzing it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a long city is measured as it is
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule seems self-evident, so why does the ברייתא state it?

steps.title: The case is a long, narrow city
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for a city that is long and narrow. We might have thought to widen it to match its length and make it a square, so the ברייתא teaches that we do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a city that is long and thin. You might have said we should give it a width as big as its length. The ברייתא teaches us that we don't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'פשיטא' question by pointing to a case where the rule is not obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the ברייתא adds corners to a round city to make it square, we might think a very thin city should also be squared off by widening it to its full length. The ברייתא says no: a long city keeps its real width, and only its actual shape counts.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for: introduces the special case a rule is really about
That is long and narrow
You might have said: introduces the mistaken assumption
Width
It teaches us: the rule comes to reject that assumption

phrases.english: It is needed only where the city is long and narrow.

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: לִיתֵּן לַהּ פּוּתְיָא אַאוּרְכַּהּ.
phrases.english: You might have said: let us give it a width equal to its length.
phrases.notes: That would turn the city into a large imaginary square.

phrases.english: So it teaches us that we do not.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: A long, narrow city should be widened to match its length.
steps.terutzMaskana: A long city keeps its real width; we do not widen it.

steps.title: Isn't the rule for a square city obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'a square city gets no added corners' and again asks why this needed saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: A square city: we don't add corners to it. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the ברייתא and asks the same 'פשיטא' question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A square already has corners, so there seems to be nothing to add. The גמרא wants to know what new point this line teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Square-shaped
Corners

phrases.english: A square city: we do not make corners for it.
That is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: מְרוּבַּעַת אֵין עוֹשִׂין לָהּ זָוִיּוֹת. פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as step 8, applied to the next line of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a square city gets no added corners
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A square already has corners, so the rule seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The case is a square that is turned at an angle
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for a square city that does not line up with north, south, east and west. We might think to turn it to face the directions, so the ברייתא teaches that we do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a city that is square but not lined up with the directions of the world. You might have said we should line it up with the world's directions. The ברייתא teaches us that we don't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second 'פשיטא' with another special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tilted square, set like a diamond against the compass, could be boxed into a bigger square that faces north-south-east-west, and that would add corner areas. The ברייתא rules that a square city is measured as it actually stands, without being re-aligned.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'square of the world': alignment with north, south, east and west
Is square

steps.confusionAlert: 'Square' here is not only about the city's shape but about its direction. The city really is square; the question is only whether its sides face the compass directions.

phrases.english: It is needed only where the city is square,
but not squared with the directions of the world.
You might have said: let us square it with the directions of the world.
So it teaches us that we do not.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דִּמְרַבְּעָא, וְלָא מְרַבְּעָא בְּרִיבּוּעַ עוֹלָם
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A tilted square city should be re-aligned to the compass directions, enlarging it.
steps.terutzMaskana: A square city is measured as it stands, without re-alignment.
steps.whyThisMatters: In step 5 a round city does get corners. Steps 9 and 11 set the limits of that idea: a city that already has a clear shape is not reshaped to make it bigger.

steps.title: Why mention two protruding houses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line about one or two protruding houses and asks: if even one house extends the line, two houses obviously do, so why say both?
steps.simpleTranslation: If one house stuck out like a turret, or two houses stuck out like two turrets. Now, if you said this about one house, do you even need to say it about two houses?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא re-quotes the protruding-house line from step 6, this time in order to question its wording. It challenges the extra phrase about two houses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One house is the weaker case for extending the line. If even one house is enough, then two houses are certainly enough, so the ברייתא's mention of two looks unnecessary. The next step answers this challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Now: introduces a 'how much more so' argument
Is it necessary? Points out that the second case is redundant
You said

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה בַּיִת אֶחָד יוֹצֵא כְּמִין פִּגּוּם
phrases.english: If one house was sticking out like a turret

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שְׁנֵי בָתִּים יוֹצְאִין כְּמִין שְׁנֵי פִגּוּמִין.
phrases.english: or two houses were sticking out like two turrets.
Now, if you said this about one house,
do you need to say it about two houses?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא בַּיִת אֶחָד אָמְרַתְּ, שְׁנֵי בָתִּים מִיבַּעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the line-by-line analysis of the ברייתא, moving to the protruding-house clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's mention of two protruding houses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If one house extends the city line, two houses surely do; the second case seems redundant.

steps.title: Two houses sticking out on two different sides
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא needed to mention two houses because they stick out on two different sides of the city. Without this, we might think we only extend the city's line for one side.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for a case of two sides. You might have said: when a house sticks out on one side we extend the line, but when houses stick out on two sides we do not. So the ברייתא teaches us that we extend on both sides.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 12. The ברייתא mentions 'two houses' because it means one house sticking out on each of two different sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was that two houses are obviously no less than one. The answer changes the picture: the two houses are not on the same side but on two different sides. We might have thought that extending the city's border on two sides at once is too much. The ברייתא teaches that each side is extended.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for... (introduces a specific case where the rule is not obvious)
Sides or directions of the city
Lest you say / you might have thought
It teaches us (the new point)

phrases.english: It is needed only for a case of two sides.
phrases.notes: One house sticks out on each of two different sides.

phrases.english: You might have said:
From one side we say [the line is extended],
from two sides we do not say so.
So it teaches us [that we extend on both sides].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12 about why both one and two houses are mentioned.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (לא צריכא): two houses on two different sides
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We extend the city's line for a protruding house on one side only, not on two sides at once.
steps.terutzMaskana: Protruding houses extend the city's measured line on every side where they appear, even on two sides.

steps.title: A city shaped like a bow or a gamma
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if a city is shaped like a bow or like the letter gamma, we treat the empty inside as if it were full of houses and courtyards. Then we measure 2,000 אמות from there.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the city was built like a bow or like a gamma, we look at it as if it were filled with houses and courtyards. Then one measures 2,000 אמות out from there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the bow-or-gamma line of the ברייתא from step 7 and quotes it again. This time it is quoted for analysis, as a setup for רב הונא's comment in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The open space inside the curve or corner is treated as part of the city, as though it were built up. So the 2,000-אמה תחום starts from the outer edge of that filled-in shape, not from the actual houses. This gives the residents more room to walk on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: A bow (a curved, arc-shaped city)
Gamma, the Greek letter Γ (a city bent at a right angle)
We view it as if
2,000 אמות, the standard תחום שבת

phrases.english: If it was made like a kind of bow
or like a kind of gamma,
phrases.notes: The Greek letter Γ: two sides meeting at a corner.

phrases.english: we view it as if
it is full of houses and courtyards,
and one measures 2,000 cubits from there and onward.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיְתָה עֲשׂוּיָה כְּמִין קֶשֶׁת אוֹ כְּמִין גַּאם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the same ברייתא after finishing the protruding-houses discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bow-shaped or gamma-shaped city is treated as if its empty inner space were filled in, and the 2,000 אמות are measured from that outer line.

steps.title: רב הונא limits the bow rule to 4,000 cubits
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says the bow-shaped city is filled in only if its two ends are less than 4,000 אמות apart. Then we measure from the imaginary bowstring. Otherwise we measure from the bow itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: for a city shaped like a bow, if the distance between its two ends is less than 4,000 אמות, we measure from the bowstring. If not, we measure from the bow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא adds a limit to the ברייתא's bow rule. The filling-in only applies when the two tips of the bow are fairly close together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each tip of the bow has its own 2,000 אמות. If the tips are less than 4,000 apart, those two areas overlap and touch, so the whole space is seen as one. Then we draw a straight line (the יתר, the bowstring) between the tips and measure from it. If the tips are 4,000 or more apart, there is no overlap, so we measure only from the actual curved houses.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, the student of רב
Bowstring: the imaginary straight line between the two ends of the bow
Its ends (the two tips of the bow)
4,000 אמות, double a תחום

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think we measure 2,000 אמות from the tips of the bow inward. The 4,000 number is only a test. It checks whether the two tips' תחומין overlap, which decides whether we may draw the bowstring.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
A city that is made like a bow,
if there is between its two ends
less than four thousand cubits,
we measure for it from the bowstring,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו — מוֹדְדִין לָהּ מִן הַקֶּשֶׁת.
phrases.english: and if not, we measure for it from the bow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: עִיר הָעֲשׂוּיָה כְּקֶשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ברייתא's bow rule from step 14 to cases where the ends are less than 4,000 אמות apart.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bow-shaped city: under 4,000 אמות between the ends, measure from the יתר; 4,000 or more, measure from the קשת itself.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling sets a 4,000-אמה gap as what separates the ends. The next step challenges exactly that number.

steps.title: רב הונא elsewhere says 141⅓ cubits is enough to split a city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב הונא could say 4,000 אמות. He also said that a breached city wall stays one city only up to a gap of 141⅓ אמות, so a much smaller gap splits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רב הונא really say this? But רב הונא said: a city wall that was broken through stays one city if the gap is up to 141⅓ אמות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction between two statements of רב הונא. One says a 4,000-אמה gap separates a city. The other says a gap of just over 141⅓ אמות already splits it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the breached wall case, a gap wider than 141⅓ אמות turns the city into two separate places. So why, in the bow case, does רב הונא let the ends be up to 4,000 אמות apart and still treat the city as one? The two numbers seem inconsistent.

keyTerms.meaning: Did רב הונא really say so? (opens a contradiction)
But didn't he say...?
A city wall that was breached
141⅓ (אמות)

phrases.english: And did Rav Huna say this?
But didn't Rav Huna say:
A city wall that was breached
[remains one city] up to 141⅓ [cubits]?
phrases.notes: A wider breach splits the city into two separate places.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַב הוּנָא הָכִי, וְהָאָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's 4,000-אמה ruling from step 15 using another ruling of his.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's statement that the ends of a bow-shaped city stay connected unless they are 4,000 אמות apart.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction between two rulings of the same אמורא. If 141⅓ אמות already separates two parts of a city, then 4,000 should not be needed.

steps.title: One side versus two sides
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר עולא answers that there is no contradiction. The 4,000 rule is where the gap is on only one side. The 141⅓ rule is where the city is broken apart on two sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר עולא said: this is not difficult. Here (4,000) the gap is on one side. There (141⅓) the break is from two sides.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר עולא resolves the contradiction from step 16. He shows that the two rulings of רב הונא deal with different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the bow city, the two ends are still joined on the other side by the built-up curve. Only one side is open, so a big gap (up to 4,000) is still treated as one city. In the breached wall case, the gap cuts through the city on two sides and really divides it in two. So a much smaller gap of 141⅓ אמות is enough to separate it.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who answers the contradiction
It is not difficult (there is no contradiction)
Here... there (each ruling applies to a different case)

steps.whatToRemember: A bow-shaped city stays one unit up to 4,000 אמות between its ends, because it is still connected on one side. A city split through on two sides is separated by a gap of more than 141⅓ אמות.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר עוּלָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Ulla said: It is not difficult:
here, it is on one side,
phrases.notes: The bow city: open only on one side, still joined by the curve.

phrases.english: there, it is from two sides.
phrases.notes: The breached wall: the city is cut through on two sides.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר עוּלָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing cases (כאן... כאן): one-sided gap versus two-sided split
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both of רב הונא's numbers measure the same kind of gap, so they contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: 4,000 אמות applies to a gap open on one side only. 141⅓ applies to a city broken apart on two sides.

steps.title: Why would רב הונא repeat a rule he already taught?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's breached-wall rule as redundant. Giving a קרפף to each section, which is where 141⅓ comes from, is something רב הונא already said on a משנה. The גמרא starts to quote that משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is he teaching us? That we give a קרפף to this section and a קרפף to that section? But רב הונא already said that one time, as we learned in a משנה:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב הונא needed to state the 141⅓ rule at all, since he already taught the same idea elsewhere. The line ends with 'דתנן', which sets up a quote from a משנה that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 141⅓ אמות is two קרפפות of 70⅔ אמות each. So the breached-wall rule really means: give one קרפף to each half of the city, and if the gap is no wider than both together, the halves count as one city. רב הונא already applied 'a קרפף to this one and a קרפף to that one' in a משנה about two towns near each other, so the second statement looks redundant.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is he teaching us? A standard challenge that a statement adds nothing new
An area of about 70⅔ אמות added beyond a city's edge for measuring the תחום
We give a קרפף to this one and a קרפף to that one, a separate allowance for each side
One time, meaning he already said it before
As we learned in a משנה. It introduces a quote from a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the number 141⅓ in this line. The גמרא assumes you know that 141⅓ is just 70⅔ + 70⅔, two קרפפות, and that is why it calls the rule 'a קרפף to this and a קרפף to that'.
steps.whyThisMatters: The challenge sets up the next move. The גמרא will need to explain what new point the breached-wall rule adds beyond רב הונא's comment on the משנה.

phrases.english: And what is he teaching us?
phrases.notes: Challenges רב הונא's 141⅓ rule as adding nothing new

phrases.english: That we give a karpef to this one
phrases.notes: One 70⅔-אמה allowance for one section of the city

phrases.english: and a karpef to that one?
phrases.notes: Another 70⅔ for the other section, totaling 141⅓

phrases.aramaic: הָא אַמְרַהּ רַב הוּנָא חֲדָא זִימְנָא,
phrases.english: But Rav Huna already said it one time,
phrases.notes: He already stated this idea elsewhere

phrases.english: as we learned in a mishna:
phrases.notes: Setup: the quoted משנה begins on the next amud

steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the contradiction resolved in step 17, the גמרא now attacks the 141⅓ rule from another angle: it seems redundant.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that a breached city stays one city if the gap is up to 141⅓ אמות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 141⅓ is just two קרפפות, one for each section. רב הונא already taught 'a קרפף to this and a קרפף to that' on a משנה, so restating it here should be unnecessary.
